newsitem.title: INDIA: Texas Instruments to model chips in India.
newsitem.headline: Texas Instruments to model chips in India.

text.p: U.S.-based Texas Instruments Inc plans to develop microprocessor chips used in digital communications in India as it expands its operations in the country, a senior official said on Friday.

"This is the first time that we are doing a processor chip ground-up from scratch in India," Sham Banerji, director of digital signal processing (DSP) product development in India, told Reuters in an interview in the southern city of Bangalore.
"The silicon design will be done in India and the manufacturing elsewhere," he said.

Banerji said Texas Instruments had been using its centre in Bangalore since 1995 to develop its processors' software content, but an increased focus on digital signal chips would translate into a further expansion of chip designing in India.
The company plans to expand the number of software and electronics experts at its Bangalore facility to 500 from the 300 currently by the end of the decade, Banerji said.

Advanced mathematical calculations go into digital signal processors, which contain a high degree of software. The processors are used in making specialised chips that are key components of cellular telephones, modems and control devices in automobiles.

With growing global computer networking, digital processing will enable faster compression, storage and transmission of text, images and sound through "any kind of wired or wireless links," Banerji said.
The advanced chips can be programmed to suit customer needs, and are sold with software development tools to help customers programme the chips, he said.

The global maket for DSP products, currently around $4 billion to $5 billion per year, is expected to grow to $10 billion by the year 2000, Banerji said. Texas Instruments leads the market with a 40 percent share, he added.
Lucent Technologies, Analog Devices and Motorola make comparable products, he said.
"We see ourselves as enablers for a networked society," Banerji said. "We are starting in a big way in India in terms of programmable processors."
Bangalore, often called India's Silicon Valley, is home to thousands of software engineers who use high-speed satellite links to send software codes and designs to facilities and customers abroad.
Texas Instruments has manufacturing facilities for silicon wafers in the United States and Japan. It operates in India through a wholly owned subsidiary.
